messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sofia Martinez, a 21-year-old animator, grew up in a household where her father’s rage turned objects into weapons. She can still hear the shatter of a picture frame against the wall, the thud of a lamp, the way her mother’s voice would go quiet before the crash. That smell—cheap whiskey and metal—lingers even now, sometimes surfacing without warning while she’s working at her drawing tablet. When it does, her heartbeat spikes and the memory rushes in, more vivid and real than anything that happened five minutes ago: she is eight again, frozen in the doorway, watching him hurl a vase past her mother’s head. Before the scene completes, she shoves it away, never letting it play to the end.

Those memories don’t stay pushed down. A coworker carelessly tosses a stress ball across the office and Sofia flinches, her fists clenching. The sudden movement triggers a full-body startle, as if the object is coming for her. She has become hypervigilant, scanning every room for potential projectiles, for signs of escalation. Irritability simmers just beneath the surface; she snaps at colleagues who approach too quickly, then hates herself for it. The sound of a dropped pen in a meeting sends her pulse racing, and she excuses herself, breath shallow. After that, she finds herself unable to make even small plans for the evening—what’s the point if she can’t guarantee safety? She controls her eating strictly, believing that if she can master her body’s appetites, she might master the chaos inside. But she knows the real strategy is avoidance: she deletes old family photos from her phone, changes her route to avoid the bar where her father used to drink, and turns off movies that show any form of domestic conflict. Yet never having stayed to witness what might happen if she didn't avoid—never letting a reminder play out without a safety behaviour—her body had never received the evidence it needed; the threat remained as high and real as the day it was set.

Sofia’s sense of helplessness has grown absolute. She is certain she cannot cope with even the smallest upset—a missed deadline makes her feel hollow, as if the world is about to crack open. The people who harmed her, her father and the system that never held him accountable, remain untouched; no one faced consequences, and that injustice deepens her conviction that she is worthless and powerless. These appraisals feed right back into her avoidance. She refuses to consider relationships, avoids dating, and tells friends she’s “not ready to think about next year.” The future feels like a trap.

The cycle tightens. Her startle response keeps her on edge, and that constant threat level triggers more intrusive olfactory memories—the whiskey, the metallic tang of blood from her mother’s split lip. Each time she blocks the memory incomplete, her helplessness spikes (“I can’t even face my own past”). In turn, the negativity drives her to tighten control: fewer meals, shorter replies, no plans. Her hypervigilance exhausts her; she snaps at a client who sends a last-minute revision, then spends the rest of the day canceling weekend commitments, retreating further. The more she restricts and avoids, the more her memories intrude when she is alone at night, as if punishing her for not facing them.

It was during a Zoom meeting last week—a colleague off-screen dropped a stack of books with a crack—that Sofia screamed, ended the call, and sat shaking at her desk. The next day she could not bring herself to open her email. She is finally reaching out because she is terrified she is losing her ability to work, and she is even more terrified that she is right. She has come to believe she cannot stop bad things from happening, but for the first time, she is hoping someone might help her learn how.
